title: Creating a migration
content:
To start migrating your databases to PostgreSQL, you will have to create a migration.
Within the CYBERTEC Migrator, a migration is the top-most object that we work with. It encapsulates the following information:
source credentials target credentials schema selection Add a migration From the dashboard, navigate to the Migration page using the left-hand menu. The dashboard provides a brief overview of the amount of migrations, the current resource consumption, as well as the last five touched migrations. Click the + Add new migration button on the top-right. The list of all migrations. From here, migrations may be created, cloned and deleted. Continue by configuring your source connection.

title: FAQ
content:
Installation and Configuration How do I configure TCPS for Oracle databases? How do I generate a self-signed certificate How do I install an existing certificate? How do I configure HTTP Basic Auth? How do I set environment variables How are the stored database passwords protected Permissions What permissions does the Migrator require for Oracle Troubleshooting ORA-12637: Packet receive failed while verifying source credentials Installation and Configuration How do I configure TCPS for Oracle databases? Install sqlnet.ora and tnsnames.ora from the template files.
➜ TNS_ADMIN=./volumes/core/config/oracle/network/admin ➜ cp "$TNS_ADMIN/templates"/*.ora "$TNS_ADMIN/" Add the net service name of the secure connection to the volumes/core/config/oracle/network/admin/tnsnames.ora.
Create a client wallet containing the database server certificates and copy all wallet files to ./volumes/core/config/oracle/wallet and restart the Migrator:
➜ cp <client wallet files> volumes/core/config/oracle/wallet ➜ ./migrator down ➜ ./migrator up When creating a new migration use the Oracle net service name defined in the previous steps. The URL format is oracle://net_service_name.
Alternatively, connect directly using the protocol parameter (e.g. oracle://localhost:2484/pdb2?protocol=tcps). This requires at least the Oracle Wallet to have been set up correctly.
How do I generate a self-signed certificate Generate the certificate with migrator configure --tls self-signed-cert and restart the Migrator.
➜ ./migrator configure --tls self-signed-cert [INFO] Generating self-signed TLS/SSL certificate ➜ ./migrator up Recreating cybertec_migrator_core_db_1 ... done Recreating cybertec_migrator_core_1 ... done Recreating cybertec_migrator_web_gui_1 ... done [OK] Started on 'https://example.org' How do I install an existing certificate? Install the certificate and the private key with configure --tls cert:<file-location>, respective configure --tls key:<file-location>, and restart the Migrator. For example if you have a certificate example.org.crt and the private key example.org.key located in /tmp. The provided paths have to be absolute.
➜ ./migrator configure --tls cert:/tmp/example.org.crt [OK] Installed TLS/SSL certificate ➜ ./migrator configure --tls key:/tmp/example.org.key [OK] Installed TLS/SSL certificate key ➜ ./migrator up Recreating cybertec_migrator_core_db_1 ... done Recreating cybertec_migrator_core_1 ... done Recreating cybertec_migrator_web_gui_1 ... done [OK] Started on 'https://example.org' How do I configure HTTP Basic Auth? The Migrator’s Nginx configuration automatically enables HTTP Basic Auth if the /etc/nginx/htpasswd/.htpasswd file is present. For Docker Compose users, this volume is pre-configured. To set up authentication, create an empty file at ./volumes/web_gui/nginx/htpasswd/.htpasswd.
To add a user, run:
sh -c "echo -n 'your-username:' >> ./volumes/web_gui/nginx/htpasswd/.htpasswd" sh -c "openssl passwd -apr1 >> ./volumes/web_gui/nginx/htpasswd/.htpasswd" Restart the Migrator with ./migrator up. The GUI will now prompt for credentials on access.
How do I set environment variables The initial ./migrator install command will generate a .env file, the contents of which will be used in the core docker compose service. When editing, make sure not to alter the # —— Internal ⚠ —— section.
How are the stored database passwords protected The Migrator stores the passwords of the source and target databases encrypted with AES-256-GCM, using a random initialization vector per value. The encryption is configured with the following environment variables of the core service:
Variable Description CORE_ENCRYPTION_KEY Encryption key, exactly 32 bytes (e.g. generated with openssl rand -base64 24). If the publicly known default key is used, the Migrator logs a warning on startup. Changing the key of an existing installation makes the stored passwords unreadable. CORE_ENCRYPTION_IV Legacy, exactly 16 bytes. Only required to decrypt passwords stored by older versions (AES-256-CBC with this fixed initialization vector). They are re-encrypted automatically on startup; keep the previous value for backups of older versions. Permissions What permissions does the Migrator require for Oracle The Migrator requires the following permissions in order to introspect and migrate an Oracle database:
Permission Usage SELECT_CATALOG_ROLE Querying the system catalog SELECT ANY TABLE Migrating table data FLASHBACK ANY TABLE Migrating table data at a certain SCN Troubleshooting ORA-12637: Packet receive failed while verifying source credentials Open the file volumes/core/config/oracle/network/admin/sqlnet.ora. If it does not exist, copy it from the templates folder. Insert the line DISABLE_OOB=ON at the beginning of the file. Restart the migrator with ./migrator up.

title: Source Connection
content:
The migration creation process begins with providing general information and source connection details.
General information The migration name and description are used solely for identification purposes and can be changed at any time.
Source connection The CYBERTEC Migrator functions by querying the schema catalog of the source database. This process requires a connection string, a username and a password. Alternatively, an Oracle Wallet can be used if configured.
Connection String The connection string must adhere following format [oracle://]host[:port]/database_name[?parameter=value]
protocol optional string Declares the DBMS. Allowed values: oracle Default: oracle host required string The hostname or IP address of the target database. Ensure that the CYBERTEC Migrator can access this machine. Default: none port optional int The port on which the target database is accessible. Default: 1521 database_name required string The SID or service name of your database. Default: none parameter optional string Optional connection parameters. Multiple parameters may be split with &.
The following parameters are currently supported:
protocol (allowed values: tcp, tcps) Default: none Examples 127.0.0.1/pdb1 oracle://localhost:1521/pdb1 oracle://secure-host:2484/tcps-database?protocol=tcps Username / Password The credentials to be used with the connection string. The provided user must have certain permissions.
Verification After entering all the required information, submit the form to confirm that the CYBERTEC Migrator can establish a connection.
Important Should you encounter an error during this phase, please refer to our FAQ. Permissions In order to function, the provided user requires the following permissions on Oracle:
Permission Reason/Usage SELECT_CATALOG_ROLE Read-access to the system catalog SELECT ANY TABLE Migration of table data FLASHBACK ANY TABLE Migration of table data at a certain SCN Summary The connection to the source database is now established, and the user’s permissions have been verified as sufficient. The next step involves selecting the schemas for migration.

title: Migration Overview
content:
The migration overview provides a comprehensive snapshot of the various database objects and datatypes within migration. This tab acts as the landing page for any migration, located within the center of the screen, and is further split into two distinct sections, each offering different views and filtering options.
Database Objects The left half of the Migration Overview displays all database object types, organized by their respective stages. This categorization helps with locate objects based on their functional role within the database:
Structure Data (always empty, as the data stage only transfers table rows) Integrity Logic Not Migrated Automatically (objects that have no equivalent in PostgreSQL or are not supported yet) Each row within the table displays the amount of the respective database object types, while specific entries can be expanded to reveal further details:
Schemas: Displays counts for schemas with objects and those without. Indices: Lists the various types of indices present, including: Normal Unique Functional Domain Filtering Clicking on any database object type sets a filter in the Sidebar (TODO: Link), focusing on relevant items associated with that selection. Furthermore, using Ctrl+Left Click adds or removes items from the filter, enabling multi-selection without losing the current filter context.
Data Types The right half of the Overview tab hosts a list of all present Data Types within the migration. This list is structured to allow for easy navigation and exploration:
Expandable Data Types: Data types with various incarnations can be expanded to list each variation (e.g., number, number(8), number(10,2)). Sorting Options: The list can be sorted alphabetically or by the quantity of each data type. Filtering: Clicking a specific data type automatically applies a filter within the Sidebar (TODO: Link), narrowing the view to items that correspond to columns with the chosen type.

title: Schema Selection
content:
Depending on the circumstances, databases can develop multiple schemas over time, often independent of each other.
The CYBERTEC Migrator supports selective schema migration, allowing users to choose which schemas to include in the process.
Important Objects with dependencies on unselected schemas are excluded from the migration. Each omission is listed during the Analyze step. Summary The schemas that shall be migrated have now been selected.
Upon clicking Next, a background worker will start crawling the source database’s schema catalog. In the meantime, the target connection may be configured.

title: Migration Stages
content:
The Stages tab serves as the control center for managing migration jobs within the migration. It allows for starting, stopping, and configuring migration processes, with real-time feedback on the progress and status of individual stages and tables.
Control Menu At the top of the Stages tab, a button group offers the primary controls for migration jobs:
Start Button: Initiates a new migration job. This button can be expanded to reveal additional options: Start: Starts the migration from the beginning, erasing all previous work on the target database. Resume: Resume a previously failed migration job from where it encountered an error. Rerun: Restarts the entire stage, erasing any work done on the target database as part of the stage. Continue: Resume the migration from the next stage, skipping any pending or erroneous work that would have happened in the current stage. Stop Button: This button becomes available only when a migration job is active. Pressing it aborts the current migration job, halting all progress. Options Button: This button opens a context menu with two toggle options: Abort Stage on First Error: Stops the migration job as soon as an error occurs. Pause After Each Stage: Pauses the migration at the end of each stage, awaiting the user to start a new migration job. Expanding the Start button reveals all possible modes of commencing a migration job. Available options for configuring migration jobs. Stages Progress Bar To the right of the control menu, the migration stages are displayed in sequence: structure, data, integrity, and logic. Each stage visually indicates its status through border styles and colors:
Grey Dashed Border: Indicates that the stage has not yet started or has been skipped. Blue Spinner: Signifies an active stage that is currently running. Green Border: Shows that the stage has completed successfully. Red Border: Indicates that the stage has failed. Yellow Border: Represents a stage that was aborted. Stage Options and Settings Hovering over a stage reveals additional options:
Stage Hooks: Appear to the left and right of each stage when hovered over. Pressing these icons allows the configuration of stage hooks. Data Stage Settings: Hovering over the Data stage reveals a settings icon. Selecting it opens a menu with two options: Skip: A toggle button that, when enabled, causes the Data stage to be skipped in migration jobs. SCN: A text field where an SCN (System Change Number) can be manually entered, allowing for precise control over data migration specifics. Hovering over a stage reveals the two hook buttons. Hovering over the data stage and clicking the settings icons reveals its options menu. Data Stage Progress Bar and Table Below the stages and control menu, a progress bar and a table provide additional insights into the data stage:
Progress Bar: Displays the current state of tables during migration, categorized into five states: Pending, Running, Aborted, Failed, and Successful. Tables Overview: This table lists all tables alphabetically as they are processed during the data stage. The status of each table is displayed on the right-hand side. Tables with partitions or those utilizing chunking can be expanded by clicking the small arrow on the left, which reveals partition or chunk-specific statuses. An example of a completed data stage, including a chunked HR.EMPLOYEES table.

title: Target Connection
content:
This step involves specifying the target PostgreSQL database into which the migration results will be written.
Connection String Similar to the source connection, the connection string for the target database must adhere to the following format [postgres://]host[:port]/database_name[?parameter=value]
protocol optional string Declares the DBMS. Allowed values: postgres Default: postgres host required string The hostname or IP address of the target database. Ensure that the CYBERTEC Migrator can access this machine. Default: none port optional int The port on which the target database is accessible. Default: 5432 database_name required string The name of the database within your cluster. Default: none parameter optional string Optional connection parameters. Multiple parameters may be split with &.
The following parameters are currently supported:
application_name connect_timeout keepalives sslmode Default: none Examples 127.0.0.1/postgres localhost:5432/my_db?application_name=my_app postgres://localhost/my_database?connect_timeout=10 example.org/my_database?sslmode=require&keepalives=1 Username / Password The credentials to be used with the connection string.
Verification After entering all the required information, submit the form to confirm that the CYBERTEC Migrator can establish a connection.
Important In case no connection can be established, or you simply want to introspect the source data schema, this step may be skipped by clicking the Continue anyways button. Summary After configuring the target connection, the migration creation concludes with the Analyze step.

title: Analyze
content:
During the Analyze step, the Migrator reads the system catalog of the source database and gathers information on each database object, along with their dependencies. With this data, the Migrator builds an internal representation of the source database, referred to by us as meta-data.
Upon completing this step, the Migrator generates an assessment of the meta-data, which will be available for review in the subsequent steps. Once this process is complete, the Finish button will become available. Selecting this will conclude the migration setup and take you to the migration overview screen.
Warnings In some instances, the Migrator may encounter issues resolving dependencies between database objects. If this occurs, these issues will appear on an error screen, which you can expand using the arrow in the upper-right corner. Review each entry carefully and, if necessary, report any potential issues to our team for further investigation.
Errors Occasionally, certain Oracle-specific constructs may not be fully processed, resulting in a faulty query. In such cases, the executed query and the associated error message will be displayed. Please report these incidents to our team so we can investigate and resolve the issue as promptly as possible.

title: Migration Settings
content:
The Settings tab provides configuration options for the migration, from general details to export utilities. The tab is organized into several sections, each addressing different settings categories.
General Contains basic information fields:
Name: A text field for modifying the name of the migration. Description: An optional text field for adding descriptive information about the migration. Credentials Allows configuration of authentication details for the databases involved:
Username and Password: Update the credentials for either the source and target databases. Parallel Workers Includes settings for managing concurrency during migration stages:
Data Transfers: Specify the maximum number of parallel transfers allowed during the data stage. Database Workers: Control the maximum number of parallel workers for the integrity stage. Progress Interval Progress Interval: Defines the interval, in seconds, for reporting the transfer status to the migration log. At each interval, the system logs the amount of bytes and rows transferred. Utility Generates a .zip archive containing detailed migration metadata and associated files. The exported archive includes:
manifest.json: Metadata about the migration, such as version numbers, timestamps, connection details, and unique identifiers. mappings.json: meta_data: Complete information about the source schema. user_mapping: Contains the latest revisions of user-applied changes. hooks: Contains the latest revisions of stage hooks. <migration name>: A folder named after the migration, containing subdirectories for database objects: functions, package bodies, packages, procedures, triggers, and views. These subdirectories house database object files, each containing: <object>.sql: The original source database code. <object>.sql.0: The code post automatic conversion by the Migrator. <object>.sql.<revision number>: The latest user-modified version, with the revision number indicating the state at the time of export.

title: Migration Assessment
content:
The Assessment tab analyzes how complex it is to migrate the database from Oracle to PostgreSQL. It answers the questions that matter when planning a migration:
How complex is the migration as a whole, and which schemas drive the complexity? Which Oracle features are used that PostgreSQL does not provide, and how are they resolved? Which database objects are the hotspots that deserve attention first? What should the migration team do, and in which order? The assessment deliberately does not estimate durations or costs. The effort of a migration depends on the team, the test strategy and the applications, which the Migrator can not know. Complexity is expressed by a score instead.
Complexity score Levels of detail Maximum depth Findings Rule catalog Hotspots and recommendations AI insights Printed report Automation Changes compared to previous versions Complexity score The migration complexity score ranges from 0 (trivial) to 100 (extremely complex). It is derived from effort points, an abstract unit that sums up the effort of all assessed objects:
a base effort per object (e.g. reviewing a table, testing a function), plus an effort per line of code the effort of every finding (an Oracle specific construct), counted at most five times per object, because repeated usages of the same construct are cheap to fix once the solution is known The score grows quickly for the first effort points and saturates for large databases, so that it remains comparable between small and very large migrations. A single finding of high severity raises the score to at least 25, a critical finding to at least 45, as such findings require a redesign no matter how small the database is.
Score Rating 0 – 14 Very low 15 – 34 Low 35 – 59 Moderate 60 – 79 High 80 – 100 Very high The migration overview shows the score of every migration, so migrations can be compared and prioritized.
Levels of detail The assessment is available in four levels of detail (depth). Each level contains the previous ones.
Depth Contents summary Complexity score, key figures (schemas, objects, lines of code, findings, share of effort supported by the Migrator) and the inventory of database objects standard Effort by category and schema, the 15 most relevant findings with up to 5 affected objects each, the 10 biggest hotspots and prioritized recommendations detailed All findings with all affected objects, up to 50 hotspots and a breakdown of every assessed object expert AI insights generated from the detailed assessment (requires the AI-Assistant) Choose the depth at the top of the Assessment tab. Levels above the maximum depth are disabled.
Maximum depth The maximum depth depends on the edition:
Edition Maximum depth Trial summary (only tables and views are assessed) Professional detailed Enterprise expert Operators can lower the maximum depth of an installation with the startup parameter --assessment-max-depth or the environment variable CORE_ASSESSMENT_MAX_DEPTH of the core container, e.g. to provide only a summary to a group of users. The startup parameter takes precedence over the environment variable. Neither can raise the maximum depth above the limit of the edition; the core logs a warning in that case and uses the limit of the edition.
services: core: command: ['--assessment-max-depth', 'standard'] An invalid value stops the core with an error message. On startup the core logs the effective maximum depth:
INFO assessment/init the maximum assessment depth is 'standard' Findings A finding is an Oracle specific construct detected by a rule, for example autonomous transactions, hierarchical queries, database links or columns of unsupported data types. Code of functions, procedures, packages, triggers and views is analyzed without comments and string literals. Each finding describes the problem and recommends how to solve it in PostgreSQL, and lists the affected objects.
Severity: Info, Low, Medium, High or Critical, describing the risk for the migration Automation: how the finding is resolved Automatic: handled by the Migrator Assisted: the Migrator supports the change (code transpilation, AI-Assistant, editors), but it has to be reviewed Manual: requires a redesign or rewrite Category: data types, schema, procedural code, SQL dialect, built-in packages, transactions, dynamic SQL, integration or operations The key figure share of effort supported by the Migrator is the share of effort points of automatic and assisted findings.

Hotspots are the objects with the highest effort points, each listing its findings. Links lead to the editor of the object.
Recommendations are derived from the findings and ordered by priority, e.g. to clarify the redesign of integrations before converting code, or to adapt the keys of partitioned tables before running the structure stage.
AI insights At the depth expert, Generate insights lets the AI-Assistant write an expert analysis of the assessment: an executive summary, the key risks, a migration strategy, quick wins and open questions for the application owners. The generation runs in the background and may take a few minutes; the result is stored with the assessment and included in the printed report.
Only the aggregated assessment (score, key figures, findings and names of affected objects) is sent to the configured LLM, no source code. Insights are generated by a language model and may be inaccurate; verify them independently.
Printed report Print report creates a report of the depth currently shown, which can be saved as PDF with the print dialog of the browser. The report is laid out for A4 paper with page numbers, repeating header and footer and chapters starting on a new page:
cover page and table of contents executive summary with the complexity score and key figures (including the AI executive summary at depth expert) inventory, complexity by category and schema, findings, hotspots and recommendations (depending on the depth) AI insights (depth expert) methodology of the score and contact information Note Enable Background graphics in the print dialog so that charts and colors are printed. Automation The assessment is available through the REST API, e.g. to include it in reports of other systems:
curl "https://migrator.example.com/api/meta-data/<meta-data-id>/assessment?depth=standard" The depth parameter is limited by the maximum depth. The meta-data id of a migration is part of its configuration (GET /api/migrations/<migration-id> → _links.configuration → _links.meta_data).

description:
The Assessment tab analyzes how complex it is to migrate the database from Oracle to PostgreSQL. It answers the questions that matter when planning a migration:
How complex is the migration as a whole, and which schemas drive the complexity? Which Oracle features are used that PostgreSQL does not provide, and how are they resolved? Which database objects are the hotspots that deserve attention first? What should the migration team do, and in which order? The assessment deliberately does not estimate durations or costs. The effort of a migration depends on the team, the test strategy and the applications, which the Migrator can not know. Complexity is expressed by a score instead.

title: Data Validation
content:
After the data stage, the Data Validation tab compares the migrated data of the PostgreSQL database with the Oracle database. It shows whether every row arrived correctly, and which rows are missing, additional or different.
Note The data validation is available in the Professional and Enterprise editions. Validation modes Progress Snapshot How rows are compared What is not compared Results Command line REST API Privileges Validation modes Mode Compared Speed Row counts the number of rows of every migrated table fast, one COUNT(*) per table and database Full comparison (default) the row counts and the values of every row, identified by the primary key reads all rows of both databases Start the validation with Start validation. It runs in the background, so you may leave the page and come back later.
Progress While the validation is running, a progress bar shows
the percentage and the phase: Counting rows of all tables, then Comparing rows the number of validated tables and, in the full comparison, the number of compared rows the table that is currently validated and the elapsed time The full comparison reads the rows in chunks of 5,000 rows. Cancel stops the validation after the current chunk and keeps the results of the tables validated so far. Only one validation per migration runs at a time, and the data can not be validated while a job of the migration is active.
Snapshot By default the Oracle database is read at the snapshot (SCN) of the data stage, so changes made to the Oracle database after the data stage do not show up as differences. This requires the undo data of that snapshot. If it is no longer available (e.g. ORA-01555 or ORA-08181), the current data is compared and the result shows a note.
Choose Current data to compare with the current content of the Oracle database, e.g. after a delta load outside the Migrator.
How rows are compared The full comparison orders the rows of both databases by the primary key and pages through them. For every chunk of Oracle rows it reads the PostgreSQL rows of the same key range, so rows that exist in only one of the databases are found as well. Strings are compared binary in both databases (NLS_COMP=BINARY in Oracle, COLLATE "C" in PostgreSQL).
Both databases convert the values into a comparable text, which accounts for the differences between Oracle and PostgreSQL:
Oracle data type Comparison NUMBER, FLOAT, INTEGER as exact decimal numbers (12.50 equals 12.5) BINARY_FLOAT, BINARY_DOUBLE, numbers migrated to double precision with a relative tolerance of 10-6 DATE with seconds, so a DATE migrated to date shows lost times as differences TIMESTAMP with microseconds TIMESTAMP WITH (LOCAL) TIME ZONE in UTC VARCHAR2, NVARCHAR2 exactly, empty strings equal NULL like in Oracle, NUL characters removed by the data stage are ignored CHAR, NCHAR without trailing blanks CLOB, NCLOB, BLOB by length and MD5 hash of the content RAW as hexadecimal value INTERVAL YEAR TO MONTH, INTERVAL DAY TO SECOND as number of months or seconds Large objects are hashed in the databases, so their content is not transferred. The complete content is hashed with DBMS_CRYPTO. Without the EXECUTE privilege on DBMS_CRYPTO, the length and the hash of the first 1,000 characters (CLOB) or 2,000 bytes (BLOB) are compared, and the result shows a note.
What is not compared Rows of tables without a primary key, of tables transferred with a custom data query, and of tables whose primary key contains columns that can not be ordered the same way in both databases: only the row counts are compared, the result shows a note. Columns of data types that can not be compared, e.g. LONG, BFILE, ROWID, user-defined types and JSON columns migrated to jsonb. They are listed per table with the reason. XMLTYPE columns are compared without the whitespace between tags, as the data stage transfers the XML indented. Excluded tables and columns, and global temporary tables, whose rows are private to the sessions. Results When the validation has finished, the result shows whether all tables match, the number of matching, mismatching and failed tables, and the number of missing, additional and different rows.
Table status Meaning Match the row counts are equal and no row differs Mismatch the row counts differ, or rows are missing, additional or different Error the table could not be validated, e.g. because it does not exist in PostgreSQL Pending the table was not validated, because the validation was cancelled Expand a table to see its notes, the columns that were not compared, and the first 20 differences:
Missing: the row of Oracle does not exist in PostgreSQL Extra: the row of PostgreSQL does not exist in Oracle Different: the row exists in both databases, the columns with different values are listed with both values Tip Differences are not always caused by the data transfer. They also reveal expressions that compute other values in PostgreSQL, e.g. of virtual columns you changed in the column editor. Keep in mind that Oracle treats NULL as an empty string when concatenating ('a' || NULL is 'a'), while PostgreSQL returns NULL. The Migrator translates concatenations of virtual columns accordingly, e.g. first_name || ' ' || last_name becomes nullif(coalesce((first_name)::text, '') || ' ' || coalesce((last_name)::text, ''), ''). Functions such as concat() can not be used, as generated columns only allow immutable expressions. Command line The validate command of the core validates the data on the command line and shows the progress in the terminal:
cli validate 4cb2f68b-41b1-49ef-a086-aa9255f57677 cli validate 4cb2f68b-41b1-49ef-a086-aa9255f57677 --mode row_count --format json > validation.json Option Description --mode <mode> full (default) or row_count --snapshot <snapshot> migration (default, the SCN of the data stage) or current --table <fqn...> validate only these tables, e.g. table:"HR"."EMPLOYEES" --format <format> text (default) or json Press Ctrl+C to cancel. The exit code is 0 if all tables match, 2 if differences were found or the validation did not finish, and 1 on errors. The result is stored, so it is shown in the Data Validation tab as well.
REST API Endpoint Description POST /migrations/{migration_id}/validation start a validation with {"mode": "full"} or {"mode": "row_count"}, optionally snapshot and tables GET /migrations/{migration_id}/validation the latest validation including its progress DELETE /migrations/{migration_id}/validation cancel the running validation Privileges The Oracle user of the migration needs the privileges of the data stage: SELECT and FLASHBACK on the migrated tables (or SELECT ANY TABLE and FLASHBACK ANY TABLE). EXECUTE on SYS.DBMS_CRYPTO is optional and enables the comparison of the complete content of large objects.

title: Usage
content:
Use your web browser to access the Migrator on the URL shown in the terminal with ./migrator up. In our example it would be https://localhost.
The configuration provided with this repository starts the CYBERTEC Migrator on the standard HTTPS port. The EXTERNAL_HTTP_PORT variable in the .env file (generated by ./migrator install) controls the choice of port on which the Migrator is served.
If you don’t have access to an Oracle or PostgreSQL database to test the Migrator, check out our Migrator demo database environment.

title: v3.11.0
content:
Features Add support for Oracle 11 (closes #14).
We changed the default configuration of the reverse proxy to use HTTPS.
This means you have to install a TLS/SSL certificate or create a self signed certificate, otherwise the web-server will refuse to start. To facilitate the installation of the certificate we added a new option --tls to the migrator configure command. Check out the FAQ for detailed information how to install a TLS/SSL certificate.
migrator configure --tls self-signed-cert Generate self-signed TLS/SSL certificate migrator configure --tls cert:<file-location> Install TLS/SSL certificate migrator configure --tls key:<file-location> Install private key of TLS/SSL certificate Attention
If you upgrade from a previous Migrator version you have to create the TLS/SSL certificate after upgrading to the new version, before restarting the new Migrator.
./migrator update ./migrator upgrade # Don't forget the create or install a TLS/SSL certificate ./migrator configure --tls self-signed-cert ./migrator up Add support for secured communication (TCPS) access to Oracle databases. For details check our FAQ - How do I configure TCPS for Oracle databases?.
Read meta-data of additional Oracle database object types: jobs and operators Users may provide a custom Data Query, thus manipulating the SELECT statement executed on the source database to migrate the data. A few use cases where this feature may be useful:
Migrate the table partially by filtering rows with WHERE Migrate only the table structure but no data (WHERE ROWID < 0) You want to keep the table structure, but not the data of a specific column (see screenshot above) Retrieve (and thus insert) the data in a specific ORDER BY Convert the column data of an unsupported data type into a string representation which can be “cast” into a valid PostgreSQL type via the COPY statement Improve output for erroneous SQL execution when reading Oracle meta-data.
Resolved Bugs Columns starting with SYS are not included in primary keys or unique constraints Data stage fails when column is named after an SQL reserved keywords (for example IN)

title: v3.5.0
content:
Features Several improvements in the execution of a migration: Swap execution order of Integrity and Logic stage. Having indices in the Logic stage makes it easier to test performance of views, stored procedures and triggers. Move creation of check constraints from Logic into Structure stage. Checking the data during the data bulk load is negligible compared to the time needed to re-read the table from disk in the Logic stage. As a consequence, functions are created in the Structure stage prior to tables, since they may be used by check constraints. The Logic stage re-creates the functions once again still providing the means for fast change-test round-trips. The Migration Overview was updated to reflect the changes in the migration execution: It is visible in which order the database objects are created: first schemas, then user defined types, followed by sequences, etc. Provide drill down on Indices entry to show the number of unique indices. We will enrich the Migration Overview with additional information in future releases. Enhance migration configuration: Constraint Renaming
Rename constraints in case there are naming collisions with other database objects. Improve handling of implicitly created indices via Unique Constraints or Primary Keys: Show implicitly created indices in the sidebar and the Indices view. In our example, dept_id_pk is shown in the Constraints as well as the Indices section. A hyperlink in the Indices view facilitates navigation to the constraint. Rename implicitly created indices by renaming its constraint. Log view shows detailed information about the started migration job: Improve Sidebar: Object Type Filter: add option for User Defined Types (UDT). Resolved Bugs Cloning a migration fails due to missing database object in the source database (dropped or renamed table, dropped column, etc.) Integrity stage ERROR: timeout exceeded when trying to connect Integrity stage keeps processing workers after an error even with enabled “Abort stage on first error” Resume of an aborted job fails when the Migrator core was forcefully shut down Core dump due to repeated, large error message (warn: Unable to process subpartition ... table not found) Functional index with an expression containing a number was not migrated Overview page does now show 0 database links, synonyms, packages

title: AI-Assistant
content:
The AI-Assistant (Enterprise Edition) helps with the migration of procedural code. In the code editor of functions, procedures, triggers and views
Explain describes what the code does and which Oracle specifics have to be considered in PostgreSQL Translate proposes a PostgreSQL version of the code, which may be applied to the editor with Apply Answers of a large language model may be wrong. Always review and test translated code before migrating it.
How it works Configuration Configuration file Selecting the configuration file Environment variables Reasoning models Troubleshooting The AI-Assistant also generates assessment insights: at the assessment depth expert, an executive summary, key risks, a migration strategy, quick wins and open questions are derived from the automated assessment (see Migration Assessment). Only the aggregated assessment result (score, findings, affected object names) is sent to the LLM for the insights, no source code.
How it works The Migrator core sends the code of the database object to a large language model (LLM) and shows the answer in the sidebar of the code editor. Any server implementing the OpenAI chat completions API (POST <baseUrl>/chat/completions) can be used, for example
self-hosted: vLLM, Ollama, llama.cpp server, LiteLLM hosted: OpenAI or any other OpenAI-compatible provider Important The code of the selected database object is sent to the configured LLM server. Use a self-hosted server if the code must not leave your infrastructure. Before the first use, each user has to confirm that code is sent to the LLM. The requests are sent by the core container, so the LLM server has to be reachable from there. Every exchange with the LLM server is recorded in the internal database (table llm_http_log, deleted together with the migration). The API key is never recorded.
Configuration The AI-Assistant is disabled unless an LLM server is configured, either with a configuration file or with environment variables. On startup the core validates the configuration and logs the model in use:
NOTICE llm/init the AI-Assistant uses model 'qwen3.8-27b' of provider 'h200' at 'https://llm.example.com/v1' (/config/llm.yaml) An invalid configuration (e.g. a missing file or an unknown model) stops the core with an error message describing the problem.
Configuration file The configuration file is written in YAML (JSON works as well). It lists one or more providers with their models; the Migrator uses one model at a time.
# Optional: provider and model to use (default: the first provider and its first model) default: provider: h200 model: qwen3.8-27b # Optional: maximum time to wait for an answer in milliseconds timeoutMs: 300000 providers: h200: baseUrl: https://llm.example.com/v1 apiKey: ${LLM_API_KEY} api: openai-completions authHeader: true models: - id: qwen3.8-27b name: Qwen3.8 27B (H200) reasoning: true input: [text, image] contextWindow: 262144 maxTokens: 32768 ollama: baseUrl: http://ollama:11434/v1 api: openai-completions authHeader: false models: - id: qwen2.5-coder:32b A complete example is available in apps/backend/llm.example.yaml.
Setting Required Description default.provider no Name of the provider to use. Default: the first provider default.model no id of the model to use. Default: the first model of the provider timeoutMs no Maximum time in milliseconds to wait for an answer. Default: CORE_LLM_TIMEOUT_MS (300000) providers.<name>.baseUrl yes Base URL of the OpenAI-compatible API, usually ending with /v1 providers.<name>.apiKey no API key of the provider providers.<name>.api no API of the provider. Only openai-completions (chat completions) is supported providers.<name>.authHeader no Send the API key as Authorization: Bearer <apiKey> header. Default: true providers.<name>.headers no Additional HTTP headers, e.g. for API gateways providers.<name>.models[].id yes Model name sent to the server (model of the request) providers.<name>.models[].name no Display name shown in the code editor. Default: id providers.<name>.models[].maxTokens no Maximum number of tokens of an answer (max_tokens). Default: limit of the server providers.<name>.models[].temperature no Sampling temperature. Default: 0.2 providers.<name>.models[].extraBody no Additional, server specific request parameters merged into the request body providers.<name>.models[].reasoning, input, contextWindow no Descriptive information about the model, not used by the Migrator Values may reference environment variables with ${NAME}, which keeps secrets out of the file. The core refuses to start if a referenced environment variable is not set.
Selecting the configuration file The configuration file is passed to the core with the startup parameter --llm-config or the environment variable CORE_LLM_CONFIG. The startup parameter takes precedence. The file has to be a YAML or JSON file (.yaml, .yml or .json).
node index.js --llm-config /config/llm.yaml With Docker or Podman, mount the file into the core container and pass the startup parameter as command, e.g. in a docker-compose.override.yml:
services: core: volumes: - ./llm.yaml:/config/llm.yaml:ro command: ['--llm-config', '/config/llm.yaml'] environment: - LLM_API_KEY=${LLM_API_KEY} Alternatively set CORE_LLM_CONFIG=/config/llm.yaml in the environment file of the installation.
Environment variables Variable Description CORE_LLM_CONFIG Path of the configuration file (the startup parameter --llm-config takes precedence) CORE_LLM_PROVIDER Provider of the configuration file to use (overrides default.provider) CORE_LLM_MODEL Model to use (overrides default.model); required without a configuration file CORE_LLM_API_KEY API key; overrides the API key of the selected provider CORE_LLM_BASE_URL Base URL of the LLM server, used only if no configuration file is given CORE_LLM_TIMEOUT_MS Maximum time in milliseconds to wait for an answer. Default: 300000 A single model can be configured without a file:
CORE_LLM_BASE_URL=https://api.openai.com/v1 CORE_LLM_MODEL=gpt-5-mini CORE_LLM_API_KEY=sk-... Reasoning models Reasoning (“thinking”) models are supported. The reasoning is not shown, only the final answer. Reasoning increases the response time; the request is aborted after timeoutMs. If a server allows to disable the reasoning, this can be done with extraBody, e.g. for Qwen models served by vLLM:
models: - id: qwen3.8-27b extraBody: chat_template_kwargs: enable_thinking: false If the answer is cut off, increase maxTokens so the model is able to finish its reasoning and the answer.
Troubleshooting Problems are shown in the sidebar of the code editor and logged by the core.
Code Message Solution MIG-7000 The AI-Assistant is not configured Configure an LLM server as described above MIG-7001 The LLM server can not be reached Check baseUrl and that the server is reachable from the core container (DNS, firewall, proxy). Also returned if the server does not answer within timeoutMs MIG-7002 The API key is unauthorized Check the API key and authHeader MIG-7003 The LLM server could not process the request The message of the server is shown, e.g. an unknown model or code exceeding the context window Requests that were in progress while the core restarted are reported as failed and can be started again with the retry button.

title: Code Transpilation
content:
The CYBERTEC Migrator is able to parse, analyze and transpile certain PL/SQL constructs to PL/pgSQL automatically. Each supported construct is represented by a corresponding rule.
This feature-set is under ongoing development, adding new rules wherever possible. If you have a suggestion for a new rule, please open a feature request.
CYAR-0001: AddParamlistParentheses Example CYAR-0002: ReplacePrologue Example CYAR-0003: ReplaceEpilogue Example CYAR-0004: FixTrunc CYAR-0005: ReplaceSysdate Example CYAR-0006: ReplaceNvl Example CYAR-0007: RemoveEditionable Example CYAR-0008: ReplaceNvl2 Example CYAR-0001: AddParamlistParentheses In Oracle, a procedure without parameters may omit parentheses in its definition, whereas PostgreSQL always requires them.
Example -- PL/SQL CREATE PROCEDURE proc IS ...; -- PL/pgSQL CREATE PROCEDURE proc() IS ...; CYAR-0002: ReplacePrologue The bodies of Oracle’s functions and procedures are initiated with IS|AS BEGIN ..., and have to be adapted to PostgreSQL’s AS $$ ....
Example -- PL/SQL CREATE PROCEDURE proc IS BEGIN ...; -- PL/pgSQL CREATE PROCEDURE proc AS $$ BEGIN ...; CYAR-0003: ReplaceEpilogue As the counterpart to CYAR-0002, this replaces the epilogue of Oracle functions and procedures, stripping the optional block identifier and specifying the LANGAGE.
Example -- PL/SQL CREATE PROCEDURE proc IS BEGIN ... END; -- PL/pgSQL CREATE PROCEDURE proc IS BEGIN ... END proc; $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql; CYAR-0004: FixTrunc Transpiles usages of Oracle’s trunc() function based on the argument type.
Note This rule has yet to be implemented. CYAR-0005: ReplaceSysdate Transpiles Oracle’s SYSDATE, which returns the current time of the operating system (as opposed to statement or transaction timestamp), to PostgreSQL’s clock_timestamp().
Example -- PL/SQL SELECT sysdate FROM dual; -- PL/pgSQL SELECT clock_timestamp() FROM dual; CYAR-0006: ReplaceNvl Replaces Oracle’s NVL with PostgreSQL’s coalesce.
Example -- PL/SQL SELECT nvl(dummy, 'null') FROM dual; -- PL/pgSQL SELECT coalesce(dummy, 'null') FROM dual; CYAR-0007: RemoveEditionable As PostgreSQL does not have the concept of editioning, the EDITIONABLE and NONEDITIONABLE keywords of functions and procedures are omitted.
Example -- PL/SQL CREATE EDITIONABLE PROCEDURE proc ...; -- PL/pgSQL CREATE PROCEDURE proc ...; CYAR-0008: ReplaceNvl2 Replaces Oracle’s NVL2 with a CASE statement.
Example -- PL/SQL SELECT NVL2(dummy, 1, 2) FROM dual; -- PL/pgSQL SELECT CASE WHEN dummy IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 2 END FROM dual;
